moduleTitle: The nature of God: the oneness of God and the Trinity — Father, Son and Holy Spirit

note.specFocus: Spec: Key beliefs — the nature of God: the oneness of God and the Trinity: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
note.summary:
Christianity is a monotheistic religion: Christians believe in one God. Yet they also believe that God has revealed himself as three persons — Father, Son and Holy Spirit. This belief is called the Trinity (from 'tri-unity').

The oneness of God
• Christianity inherited Jewish monotheism. The Shema says 'Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one' (Deuteronomy 6:4); Jesus quoted it as the greatest commandment (Mark 12:29–30).
• The first of the Ten Commandments forbids other gods (Exodus 20:3).
• The Nicene Creed opens: 'We believe in one God'.

The Trinity
• One God in three persons. Each person is fully God; they are distinct from one another; but there are not three gods.
• The word 'Trinity' is not in the Bible, but Christians find the idea there: Jesus' baptism (Mark 1:9–11) — the Son is baptised, the Spirit descends like a dove, the Father speaks; the Great Commission — baptise 'in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit' (Matthew 28:19); the Grace (2 Corinthians 13:14).
• The doctrine was formally defined in the Nicene Creed (Councils of Nicaea 325 and Constantinople 381).

The three persons
• God the Father: creator and sustainer of all; a loving parent ('Our Father in heaven', Matthew 6:9); 'the Father almighty' (Apostles' Creed).
• God the Son: Jesus Christ, God incarnate, fully God and fully human; 'of one Being with the Father' (Nicene Creed); 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30). He saves humanity through his death and resurrection.
• God the Holy Spirit: God's presence and power in the world today; 'the Lord, the giver of life'; came upon the disciples at Pentecost (Acts 2); guides, comforts and strengthens ('the Advocate', John 14:26); produces the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23).

Diversity of views
• The filioque ('and the Son'): Catholic and most Protestant Churches say the Spirit proceeds 'from the Father and the Son'; Orthodox Christians say 'from the Father'. This was one cause of the Great Schism of 1054.
• Pentecostal and charismatic churches emphasise the Spirit's gifts (tongues, healing, prophecy).
• A few groups outside mainstream Christianity (e.g. Jehovah's Witnesses, Unitarians) reject the Trinity.
• Analogies (shamrock, water/ice/steam, a person who is a parent, child and sibling) are popular but imperfect; the Church calls the Trinity a mystery.

Why it matters / influence
• Worship: baptism in the threefold name; the sign of the cross; doxologies ('Glory be to the Father…'); creeds recited in services.
• Prayer: often to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit.
• Relationships: the Trinity is a community of love, so Christians value community, unity and loving relationships.
• Experience: Christians feel they know God as creator, as saviour in Jesus, and as an inner presence.

Key terms: monotheism, Trinity, Father, Son, Holy Spirit, Nicene Creed, filioque, Pentecost, incarnation.

questions.question:
Which one of the following is the Christian belief that God is three persons in one?
A  The Incarnation
B  The Atonement
C  The Trinity
D  The Resurrection
questions.modelAnswer:
C — The Trinity

The Trinity is the belief that the one God exists as three distinct persons — Father, Son and Holy Spirit — each fully God, yet not three gods. The Incarnation is God becoming human in Jesus; the Atonement is the restoring of the relationship between God and humanity; the Resurrection is Jesus rising from the dead.
questions.examTip: Watch for distractors that are also key Christian terms — be sure of each definition.

questions.question:
At which event in the Gospels are all three persons of the Trinity described as present?
A  The feeding of the 5000
B  The baptism of Jesus
C  The Last Supper
D  The Ascension
questions.modelAnswer:
B — The baptism of Jesus

At Jesus' baptism in the River Jordan, the Son is baptised, the Holy Spirit descends 'like a dove', and the Father's voice says 'You are my Son, whom I love' (Mark 1:10–11; Matthew 3:16–17). Christians often cite this as a biblical picture of the Trinity.
questions.examTip: The baptism of Jesus is the classic biblical illustration of the Trinity — learn it.

questions.question: Give one name for the third person of the Trinity.
questions.modelAnswer: The Holy Spirit (also accept: the Holy Ghost / the Paraclete / the Advocate / the Comforter).
questions.examTip: Short-response items need one precise answer.

questions.question: Give one quotation or teaching that shows Christians believe in only one God.
questions.modelAnswer:
Any one of, e.g.:
• 'Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one' (the Shema, Deuteronomy 6:4, quoted by Jesus in Mark 12:29).
• 'We believe in one God' (opening of the Nicene Creed).
• 'You shall have no other gods before me' (Exodus 20:3).
questions.examTip: A short quotation with its reference is the most secure way to earn a 1-mark 'give one' teaching.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which belief in the Trinity influences Christians today.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: Christians worship God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit. For example, baptisms are carried out 'in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit' (Matthew 28:19), and many services end with the Grace or a Trinitarian blessing, so the belief shapes the words of everyday worship and prayer.

Second way: Because the Trinity is a relationship of love between the three persons, Christians believe they are made for relationships too. This influences them to value community — belonging to a church family, caring for others and seeking unity — as a reflection of God's own nature. They may also pray to the Father, through the Son, in the power of the Spirit.
questions.examTip: Show practical influence — worship, prayer, behaviour or community life.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which belief in the Holy Spirit influences Christians today.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: Christians believe the Holy Spirit guides and strengthens them, as Jesus promised the Advocate would 'teach you all things' (John 14:26). This influences them to pray for guidance when making decisions and to trust that they are not alone when facing difficulties.

Second way: Many Christians believe the Spirit gives gifts and produces 'fruit' such as love, joy, peace and patience (Galatians 5:22–23). They try to develop these qualities in daily life, and in Pentecostal and charismatic churches worshippers may expect spiritual gifts such as speaking in tongues or healing during worship.
questions.examTip: Make each influence different — don't give two versions of 'it helps them'.

questions.question:
Explain two Christian teachings about the Trinity.

Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First teaching: There is only one God, but God exists as three distinct persons — Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Christians stress they are not three gods; each person is fully God and shares the same divine nature. The Nicene Creed begins 'We believe in one God' and goes on to describe the Son as 'of one Being with the Father'.

Second teaching: Each person of the Trinity has a distinctive role. The Father is the creator and sustainer of all; the Son became human in Jesus to save humanity; the Holy Spirit is God's presence active in the world, guiding and strengthening believers. In the Nicene Creed the Spirit is 'the Lord, the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father [and the Son]'.

Source applied: Jesus commanded his followers to baptise 'in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit' (Matthew 28:19) — note 'name' is singular, which Christians see as showing the three persons are one God. (The words 'and the Son' — the filioque — are accepted by Catholic and most Protestant churches but not by the Orthodox Church.)
questions.examTip: The Nicene Creed is an excellent 'another source of Christian belief' — learn one line from it.

questions.question:
Explain two Christian teachings about God the Father and God the Son.

Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First teaching — God the Father: Christians believe the Father is the creator of the universe and a loving parent who cares for every person. Jesus taught his disciples to pray 'Our Father in heaven' (Matthew 6:9), showing a close, personal relationship. The Apostles' Creed describes him as 'God, the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth'.

Second teaching — God the Son: Jesus is the Son of God, fully divine and fully human, who became incarnate to save humanity. He is not a created being but eternally one with the Father: 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30). The Nicene Creed calls him 'eternally begotten of the Father… of one Being with the Father'.

Application: These teachings mean Christians can relate to God both as a caring parent and through Jesus, who reveals what God is like — 'Anyone who has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9).
questions.examTip: Develop each teaching with what it means for Christians, not just a description.

questions.question:
‘The Trinity is too difficult for Christians to understand.’

Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Christian teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT OF THE STATEMENT

The Trinity seems to break ordinary logic: one God who is three persons, each fully God, yet not three gods. Even great theologians have admitted it is a mystery. St Augustine wrote an entire book, De Trinitate, trying to explain it, and the Church itself calls it a mystery of faith that human reason could never discover on its own.

The word 'Trinity' does not appear in the Bible. The doctrine was defined later, at the Councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381), after centuries of argument. If the early Church took so long to agree, and the churches still disagree over details such as the filioque (whether the Spirit proceeds from the Father 'and the Son'), it is reasonable to say ordinary Christians may struggle to understand it.

Analogies often used — water as ice, liquid and steam; or a shamrock — are imperfect and can lead to errors such as modalism (one God wearing three 'masks'). Non-Christians, such as Muslims and Jews, sometimes see the Trinity as compromising belief in one God.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

Christians argue that they do not need to understand everything about God to understand enough. The basic teaching is clear: one God (Deuteronomy 6:4) who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). Christians experience God in these three ways — as creator and loving Father, through Jesus, and through the Spirit at work in their lives.

The Trinity is learned through worship rather than abstract theory. Christians are baptised in the name of the Trinity, recite the Nicene Creed, and pray the Grace (2 Corinthians 13:14). The doctrine is lived, not merely studied, so most believers understand it in practice.

Many Christians say that if God were simple enough to understand completely, he would not be God. A finite mind cannot fully grasp an infinite being, so mystery is exactly what you would expect.

JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION

It is true that the Trinity cannot be fully understood — the Church itself says so. However, the statement suggests it is 'too difficult', implying Christians cannot understand it at all. I disagree: the central idea is clearly expressed in scripture and the creeds, and Christians grasp it through worship and experience. The Trinity is a mystery to be explored rather than a puzzle to be solved, so it is difficult but not too difficult for Christian faith.
questions.examTip: Distinguish between 'understand fully' and 'understand enough' — that distinction gives a strong conclusion.

questions.question:
‘Belief in the Holy Spirit is the most important part of the Trinity for Christians today.’

Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Christian teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT OF THE STATEMENT

The Holy Spirit is God at work in the lives of Christians now. Jesus promised that after he left, the Father would send 'the Advocate, the Holy Spirit' to teach and remind believers (John 14:26). Jesus has ascended, so for Christians today it is the Spirit who brings God's presence into daily life.

The Church itself began when the Spirit came at Pentecost (Acts 2), giving the disciples courage to preach. Christians believe the Spirit continues to guide the Church, inspire scripture, give gifts and produce the 'fruit of the Spirit' (Galatians 5:22–23). Pentecostal and charismatic Christians, one of the fastest-growing groups worldwide, place particular emphasis on the Spirit's power in worship, healing and speaking in tongues.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

Christians believe the three persons are equal: no person of the Trinity is more important than another. The Athanasian Creed says 'none is before or after another; none is greater or less than another'. To make one person 'most important' could distort the doctrine.

Many Christians would say Jesus the Son is central, because salvation comes through his death and resurrection (John 3:16), and Christianity is named after Christ. The Spirit's role is to point people to Jesus (John 15:26). Others emphasise God the Father as creator, to whom Jesus himself prayed ('Our Father', Matthew 6:9).

Catholic and Orthodox Christians experience the Spirit mainly through the sacraments and the Church's tradition, rather than as a separate focus. For them the Spirit cannot be separated from the work of Father and Son.

JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION

There is a strong case that the Spirit is the person of the Trinity Christians most directly experience today, especially in Pentecostal traditions. However, Christian teaching is clear that the three persons are co-equal and work together: the Father sends, the Son saves and the Spirit makes that salvation real in believers. I therefore conclude that the Spirit is extremely important to Christians today, but it is not accurate to call it the 'most important' part of the Trinity, because that contradicts the very idea of three equal persons in one God.
questions.examTip: Use differences between Christian traditions (e.g. Pentecostal vs Orthodox) — it shows the diversity examiners reward.
